segments.text: This chapter studies how the Earth concentrates useful materials into economically extractable deposits, and how such deposits are found, quantified, and responsibly exploited — extending the ore-genesis and exploration ideas begun in Petroleum Geology (Chapter 8) to solid mineral and energy resources.
Metallic minerals

(ores of metals such as copper, iron, or gold) are valued for the extractable metal they contain, typically requiring processing (crushing, concentration, and smelting or leaching) to separate the valuable metal from waste rock (gangue).
Non-metallic minerals

(such as limestone, gypsum, or salt) are valued instead for their bulk chemical or physical properties, used directly or with comparatively simple processing (for example, in construction materials, chemical manufacturing, or agriculture) — this distinction shapes both the economics and the typical exploration approach appropriate to each.

blocks.text: 2. Coal and other geological energy resources

segments.text: Coal

forms from the burial and progressive compaction/alteration of accumulated plant material in ancient swamp environments, with increasing burial depth, time, temperature, and pressure driving it through a recognised rank sequence (peat, through lignite and bituminous coal, to anthracite) — higher rank coal has progressively higher carbon content and, correspondingly, higher energy content per unit mass. Beyond coal and petroleum (Chapter 8), other geological energy resources include natural gas (often associated with petroleum systems but also occurring independently), geothermal energy (harnessing naturally occurring subsurface heat, most viable in tectonically and volcanically active regions), and radioactive minerals (uranium ore, providing fuel for nuclear energy).
Ore genesis

explains the specific geological process that concentrated a valuable material to economically viable levels, since most useful elements occur only at very low, non-economic background concentrations throughout ordinary rock. Major recognised deposit types include
magmatic deposits
(valuable minerals concentrate directly by crystallising from and settling within a cooling magma body),
hydrothermal deposits
(hot, mineral-rich fluids circulate through rock fractures, depositing valuable minerals as they cool or react chemically with the surrounding rock), and
sedimentary/placer deposits

(dense, physically or chemically resistant valuable minerals become naturally concentrated by ordinary sedimentary sorting and transport processes, such as gold or heavy mineral sands concentrating in a stream bed). Correctly classifying a given deposit by its genetic process is the essential first step in predicting its likely size, shape, and grade distribution.

Mineral exploration follows a similarly progressive, uncertainty-reducing workflow to petroleum exploration (Chapter 8): beginning with broad regional reconnaissance (using existing geological maps and regional-scale geochemical or geophysical surveys, Chapter 6, to identify promising target areas), narrowing to detailed local geological mapping and more focused geochemical/geophysical surveying (to precisely define specific drilling targets within the identified promising areas), then diamond or other core drilling (to directly sample and confirm the subsurface presence, extent, and grade of mineralisation), and finally detailed economic evaluation (point 5) of any deposit confirmed by drilling.

blocks.text: 5. Resource and reserve concepts and responsible extraction

segments.text: A geological
resource
is material known or estimated to exist in the ground, of potential economic interest, but not automatically economically extractable under current conditions. A
reserve

is specifically the portion of a resource that has been demonstrated (through the exploration and evaluation workflow above) to be both technically and economically extractable under current, specifically stated economic and technical conditions — since a reserve estimate depends explicitly on assumed prices, costs, and available extraction technology, the same physical deposit’s classified reserve size can change over time even without any new drilling, simply because economic or technical conditions have changed.
Responsible extraction

requires appropriately balancing genuine economic benefit against environmental impact (Chapter 9) and the long-term sustainable, non-renewable use of the resource, since mineral deposits, unlike some other natural resources, do not regenerate on human timescales.

Pakistan hosts several nationally and, in some cases, regionally significant mineral occurrences, including notable copper-gold porphyry deposits (such as at Saindak and Reko Diq in Balochistan) and substantial coal resources (such as the Thar coalfield in Sindh) — because specific reserve and production figures for these deposits are genuinely subject to ongoing change as exploration continues and extraction proceeds, current, accurate figures should always be verified against the latest Geological Survey of Pakistan, relevant government ministry, or regulatory/company technical report publications, rather than relied upon as static facts.

items.text: Metallic minerals are valued for extractable metal content (requiring processing); non-metallic minerals are valued for bulk chemical/physical properties, generally used with simpler processing.
Coal’s rank sequence (peat to anthracite) reflects increasing burial depth, time, temperature, and pressure, with higher rank meaning higher carbon and energy content.

Magmatic, hydrothermal, and sedimentary/placer processes are the three major ore-genesis categories, and correctly classifying a deposit’s genesis predicts its likely size, shape, and grade characteristics.
Mineral exploration follows a progressively narrowing, uncertainty-reducing workflow from regional reconnaissance through detailed mapping/surveying to drilling and economic evaluation.

A resource is potentially economic material in the ground; a reserve is specifically the technically and economically extractable portion under stated current conditions, meaning reserve classifications can change without new drilling; current Pakistani figures should be verified against official Geological Survey of Pakistan or government sources.
